sections.title: Identification
sections.text: Amanita citrina has a 4–10 cm ivory to pale lemon cap, sometimes wholly white, rounded at first and later flattening. Irregular whitish or yellowish patches of the universal veil may remain on its surface. The crowded gills are white and free. A usually persistent membranous ring hangs from the pale stem. The base has a large abrupt bulb with an adherent volval rim rather than a loose basal sack. A raw-potato smell is most evident in cut young fruitbodies and can fade with age.

sections.title: Habitat and season
sections.text: An ectomycorrhizal woodland species with broadleaved and mixed trees, often oak and beech, and also conifers. It fruits on the ground, often in late summer and autumn. Abundance varies by region and habitat.

sections.title: Dangerous look-alikes
sections.text: The pale yellow form can resemble a young death cap, while the white form can resemble a destroying angel. All may show pale gills and a ring. Cap patches, smell and the bulb's rim help describe a complete specimen, but vary or may disappear; none alone makes a collection safe. Expose the entire stem base to inspect its volva.

sections.title: Toxicity
sections.text: The German Mycological Society lists A. citrina for gastrointestinal poisoning and notes bufotenin. It also reports poisoning after heating, so cooking does not make it reliably safe. Other guides describe it as inedible or mildly toxic; that disagreement offers no reason to eat it given the possibility of confusing it with deadly amanitas.

traits: Ivory to pale lemon cap, sometimes white, with irregular veil patches
Usually persistent membranous ring on a pale stem
Large abrupt bulb with adherent volval rim, without a free sack
Raw-potato smell especially when young, variable with age
safetyNote: Do not eat Amanita citrina. The DGfM reports digestive poisoning, including after heating. Its resemblance to deadly amanitas demands caution; seek prompt poison-centre or medical advice after suspected ingestion.
